5.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
5.title: Which report to use
5.content: All three reports come from the same calibrated model and the same calculations. | InverseAudit - The usual report. It needs no site visit, so it suits remote screening, owner reports and planning. | ASHRAE Level 1 - What ASHRAE Standard 211 asks for a Level 1 audit: a site visit, a description of the building, the historical energy use with the benchmark and target, and the measure summary of low-cost and capital measures, with InverseAudit’s executive summary and utility analysis. It leaves out InverseAudit’s measure-by-measure results, which are Level 2’s. Use it when a program asks for a Level 1 audit only: the auditor has far fewer entries to make (about a third as many). | ASHRAE Level 2 - Level 1 plus what the standard asks for a Level 2 audit: the building’s systems (envelope, HVAC, water heating, lighting and loads), an equipment inventory, the end use breakdown, and more about each measure and the package. Use it when a program asks for a Standard 211 Level 2 audit, for example C-PACE financing, LEED O+M or a city’s audit ordinance. | . The standard doesn’t cover remote audits: every level needs a site visit by a qualified energy auditor. InverseAudit’s analysis alone isn’t a Standard 211 audit, which is why an ASHRAE report stays a draft until the auditor’s entries are done. When no program asks for the standard, see If the project doesn’t need to meet Standard 211.

6.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
6.title: Choose the report
6.content: . | On Energy Auditing, choose the building. | Next to Download PDF, click ASHRAE Level 1 or ASHRAE Level 2 under Report. | Click Use ASHRAE Level 1 or Use ASHRAE Level 2 to confirm. | . The page reloads with a Site visit tab, and the Download PDF menu lists the ASHRAE report’s parts. Each building keeps its own report type, and new buildings start on InverseAudit. You can switch at any time. The site visit entries are shared by both levels, so moving from Level 1 to Level 2 keeps everything entered and adds Level 2’s entries; moving back keeps Level 2’s entries without printing them. Only the building’s analyzer can switch, and not while the audit is posted: unpost it first. What Level 1 leaves out . At Level 1 the Site visit tab hides Envelope, Water heating, lighting, loads and Equipment inventory. HVAC asks only for the building automation, and Measures and package only for measures without calculated savings. Items to verify are optional, and Facility and contacts doesn’t ask for the building shape or the walls by facing. The Level 1 report’s Analysis is only the baseline model’s energy use by end use, and its Recommendations are only the measure summary: InverseAudit’s before-and-after end-use analysis, monthly costs and use, measure tables, utility rates, savings table and measure write-ups are left out, because a Level 1 audit doesn’t calculate each measure. The Analysis and Recommendations PDFs are the same. The measures are still entered and calculated on the Energy Auditing page, and the measure summary uses their figures. The Level 1 report also leaves out Level 2’s pages: Building envelope, HVAC systems, Water heating, lighting and other loads, Equipment inventory, the walls by facing, the End-use breakdown, Renewable and distributed energy, and Level 2’s Recommendations pages (the review with the owner, the cost breakdown, the Level 2 measure summary, the savings by measure and the QA/QC check, the package, M&V and Level 3). Its cover and compliance form say Level 1.

7.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
7.title: If the project doesn’t need to meet Standard 211
7.content: Some clients want the ASHRAE report’s pages without a Standard 211 audit, for example when the audit is remote. On the Site visit tab, open Compliance page and untick This project must meet ASHRAE Standard 211. The box is ticked unless you untick it. With the box unticked: . | Every site visit entry is optional. The entries you make are printed and empty ones aren’t, so the report is never a draft. Each section shows how many entries are made instead of how many are left. | Missing bills don’t make the report a draft. The historical energy use pages still say which bills are missing. | The report doesn’t name Standard 211. The cover says “Level 2 energy audit” (or Level 1), and so does the audit overview. The auditor’s statement certifies that the report is complete and correct, and mentions a site visit only if its date is entered. The tables keep the standard’s layout, but their notes don’t refer to its forms. | The compliance form (Form A) is left out, and so are the entries only it uses: the qualification route, the audits completed and, at Level 2, the Level 1 date. In Download PDF, Cover and compliance becomes Cover page. | . You can tick the box again at any time, and nothing you entered is lost. Like the other entries, it locks while the audit is posted.

8.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
8.title: The Site visit tab
8.content: The qualified energy auditor fills in the Site visit tab after visiting the building. Its sections are listed on the left, each with how many of its entries are done: . | Site visit and interviews - The dates, who was there, the areas and systems visited, what was checked, the interviews, operation and maintenance observations, and the main findings for the Executive summary. | Items to verify - What the owner entered and what the calibration found, for the operating hours, setpoints, lighting, heating, cooling, outside air and water heating. Tick Confirmed when the site visit agrees, or write what was found. | Facility and contacts - Renovations, earlier audits, landmark status, the owner and bill payer, other space types, the occupancy schedule, and the walls on each side of the building. | Envelope, HVAC and Water heating, lighting, loads - What the model can’t know, such as construction, condition, controls and nameplates. | Equipment inventory - The units installed, one row for each unit or group of identical units. | Utility accounts and rates - Account and meter numbers, and the tariffs. | Measures and package - The review with the owner, planned dates, reasons for measures not evaluated, funding, O&M and M&V costs, and the assessment of solar PV and combined heat and power. | Compliance page - Whether the project must meet ASHRAE Standard 211, the building owner, the auditor and their qualification, and the dates the Level 1 and Level 2 audits were completed. | . Each entry saves when you leave it. For tables, click Add a row to add a row and × to remove one. The entries lock while the audit is posted, and only the building’s analyzer can change them. The number on the tab is how many entries are still empty. An entry left empty isn’t printed, and neither is its title. A table or column with nothing else in it is left out too. The exception is the compliance form (Form A): it keeps all its lines, blank where nothing is entered, so it can be filled in by hand. Narratives . Envelope, HVAC and Water heating, lighting, loads each have narratives for describing the building as found, for example “Systems installed” for the HVAC. They’re optional, so a narrative left empty doesn’t keep the report a draft. Measure text and priorities . The reports use InverseAudit’s text for each kind of measure: its comfort, other non-energy and O&M impacts and, at Level 1, the system it changes. Under Measures and package, the auditor can replace that text for this building, and at Level 1 a measure’s priority. The measure summary with Low, Medium and High bands and a priority is Level 1’s form (L1 - EEM Summary). The Level 2 report has the standard’s Level 2 form instead (L2 - EEM Summary), with each measure’s savings, cost, life, ROI and payback. It opens the Recommendations section, as the same table does in the InverseAudit report, where only the non-energy cost savings column is left out. The comfort and other non-energy impacts are in the Level 2 report’s Other impacts and planned dates table.

9.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
9.title: What the report adds
9.content: | Where | What | . | Cover | The Standard 211 Level 2 title, the site visit date and the auditor’s statement | . | After the cover | The compliance form (Form A) | . | Executive summary | An audit overview at the top: scope, energy data, method, key dates, contacts, energy use and the recommended package | . | New sections after the Executive summary | Site visit and interviews, Facility description, Building envelope, HVAC systems, Water heating, lighting and other loads and Equipment inventory | . | Analysis | Opens with energy use by end use with all fuels, before and after the measures, and the End-use breakdown of each fuel with each end use’s peak kW, in place of InverseAudit’s electricity end-use charts and tables. Ends with Renewable and distributed energy. The utility rates are in Historical energy use | . | Recommendations | The Level 2 measure summary (the standard’s L2 - EEM Summary) at the top, in place of InverseAudit’s recommendations table, then the measure write-ups, the review with the owner, the cost breakdown (material, labor and markup), the other impacts and planned dates, measures considered but not recommended, the savings by measure and end use with the QA/QC check, the recommended package, where the savings come from, measurement and verification, and measures for a Level 3 analysis | . | Utility analysis | Historical energy use (accounts, rates, the measured data and the benchmark) and Calibration results. A bill whose cost isn’t on the meter data is estimated in grey at the average rate: the year’s cost ÷ use at the building’s rates. InverseAudit’s EUI and costs by year come first only when the building has more than one year of data | . Each figure is marked with where it comes from: Model (the building’s inputs and model), Modeled, verify (estimated by the calibration, for the auditor to check), Calculated, or Auditor. Equipment as the model’s totals . The calibrated model simplifies the building’s geometry and systems; for example, it may have one air handler per floor. So the report gives equipment as the model’s totals, such as the total cooling capacity, supply air and fan power. The auditor lists the units actually installed in the equipment inventory, and the report adds up their nameplate capacities next to the model’s totals.

10.title: Draft until it’s complete
10.content: While any required site visit entry is empty, or the energy data is incomplete (for example, natural gas is used but there are no gas bills), the report is a draft: . | Empty entries don’t print, so the Site visit tab is where to see which are open. | Every page header says DRAFT, with how many site visit items are open and what data is missing. | The compliance form shows Not yet for the standard’s requirements, and its signature lines are marked not to be signed. | Full report in the Download PDF menu shows how many items are open. | . Enter 12 months of bills for each fuel on the building’s meter data to complete the energy data. See Meter data.

11.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
11.title: Download the PDFs
11.content: Under Download PDF, both ASHRAE reports have Full report, Cover and compliance, Executive summary, Site visit and facility, Analysis, Recommendations, Utility analysis and, for US buildings, Appendix A: ESG/carbon. The parts show the same pages as in the full report. The full report leaves out Appendix B (the carbon impact of each measure), which the standard doesn’t ask for; it stays in InverseAudit’s report and on the Recommendations tab. See Reports and PDFs.

12.title: What the auditor still decides
12.content: . | Measures without calculated savings - Keep each, with the reason, or drop it. | Measures not evaluated - Where the building is below the energy code and no measure was run, give the reason. 14.title: Calculate, update and post
14.content: Try measures on the calibrated model, refresh the report with the results, and post it for your contacts and clients. For: AnalyzerTakes: A few minutes per runWhere: Analysis › Energy Auditing › Measures panel . The building is calibrated, pinned and subscribed. See Run an energy audit.

15.title: Steps
15.content: . | In the Measures panel, choose the measures you want to apply by changing their values. | Click Calculate. InverseAudit runs the simulation with the selected measures and shows the new savings. The report is marked “The report is outdated”. | If the savings meet your expectations, click Update. The report is updated with the new results. This runs an energy simulation for each measure and can take several minutes. | Optionally, click Run AI analysis to rewrite the report’s text with AI. This replaces the text of every report section, including text you edited yourself. | Check the report. If everything is in order, click Post. | .

16.title: When the buttons turn on
16.content: Each time you open the Energy Auditing page, Update, Run AI analysis and Post start grayed out. | Update turns on when a Calculate finishes. | Post and Run AI analysis turn on when an Update finishes. Post also turns on when Run AI analysis finishes. | After Unpost, run Calculate and Update again before you can post. | . To post an audit you updated during an earlier visit, run Calculate and Update again.

17.title: What you’ll see next
17.content: Your client can view the posted report (see What clients see), and the building appears in Portfolio. The Utility analysis tab of the report becomes available. After the audit is posted, Calculate is turned off. To make changes, click Unpost first. Unpost appears only after the audit has been posted.

18.title: If something goes wrong
18.content: "The report is outdated" You calculated new measures but haven’t refreshed the report yet. Click Update in the Measures panel. "Some text in this section was written from older results" The text was written before the last Update, or before the results changed in some other way, for example a new calibration or new utility rates. Its numbers may not match the tables. Click Run AI analysis to rewrite it, or edit the text. Post asks about it too. Text saved before November 2026 is checked against the last Update only. Calculate shows an error Click Calculate again. If the error comes back, contact support with the building’s name. Update or Post is grayed out They turn on only after Calculate (for Update) and Update (for Post) finish during the current visit. See When the buttons turn on. Calculate shows "Complete Your Energy Audit" The building isn’t subscribed. The Energy Auditing page also shows a Not subscribed banner. Subscribe the building, then calculate again. Calculate is grayed out The audit is posted, or you aren’t the building’s analyzer. If it’s posted, click Unpost first.

20.title: Read the calibration results
20.content: How to tell whether the calibrated model is accurate enough, using its goodness of fit. Where: Home › Building setup › Stats and the top of the Benchmarking page .

21.title: Goodness of fit
21.content: If a model is calibrated within the threshold limits, it is considered sufficiently accurate in simulating the physical reality it is intended to represent. These thresholds are a preliminary guide for the building calibration and should not be treated as absolute values. The statistical indices here relate only to the predicted building energy consumption. | CV(RMSE) - How much the model’s hourly or monthly values scatter around the measured values. | NMBE - Whether the model uses more or less energy than measured, on average. | .

22.title: Hourly calibration
22.content: Threshold limits of statistical criteria for calibration: . | Statistical Indices | ASHRAE Guideline 14 | IPMVP | FEMP | . | NMBE [%] | ±10 | ±5 | ±10 | . | CV(RMSE) [%] | 30 | 20 | 30 | . | CV(RMSE) | Less than 20% | Between 20% and 30% | Greater than 30% | . | Calibration | Good-fitting | Acceptable | Not acceptable | . | Required procedure | Not required | Not required | Double-check meter data and user inputs and then rerun a calibration | .

23.title: Monthly calibration
23.content: Threshold limits of statistical criteria for calibration: . | Statistical Indices | ASHRAE Guideline 14 | IPMVP | FEMP | . | NMBE [%] | ±5 | ±20 | ±5 | . | CV(RMSE) [%] | 15 | - | 15 | . | CV(RMSE) | Less than 8% | Between 8% and 15% | Greater than 15% | . | Calibration | Good-fitting | Acceptable | Not acceptable | . | Required procedure | Not required | Not required | Double-check meter data and user inputs and then rerun a calibration | .

24.title: On the Benchmark page
24.content: The Benchmarking page shows the same two values as bars. The dark mark is the ASHRAE Guideline 14 limit, and the bar turns orange when the value goes past it. The label next to the bars shows whether the calibrated model meets the guideline.

26.title: Check inputs and run calibration
26.content: The calibration tunes your building’s energy model until it matches your meter data. Every benchmark and audit result comes from the calibrated model. For: AnalyzerTakes: 3 to 40 minutesWhere: Home › Building setup . | All four cards on the building are complete: Meter data, Geometry, Systems and Rates. None shows a Pending badge. | You are the building’s analyzer. Other people see the panel in view-only mode. | .

27.title: Steps
27.content: . | On Home, click the building’s card. In the Building setup panel, click Check inputs. The check takes a few seconds and covers your inputs, historical weather data, incentive rates and retrofit costs. Anything that needs fixing is listed on the Issues tab. | When the check passes, the button changes to Run calibration. Choose a Calibration length: . | Quick - About 3 minutes. | Standard - About 20 minutes. Recommended. | Thorough - About 40 minutes. Tests more combinations of model inputs. | . | To get an email when it’s done, check Send me an email when ready. Then click Run calibration and confirm with Run Calibration. | .

28.title: What you’ll see next
28.content: You can leave the page while the calibration runs. The button shows its progress, for example Calibration in progress (45%). When it finishes, it shows Calibration complete, and the Stats tab shows how closely the model matches your meter data: . | Meter data | CV(RMSE) | NMBE | . | Hourly | 30% or less | within ±10% | . | Monthly | 15% or less | within ±5% | . These are the ASHRAE Guideline 14 limits. See Read the calibration results. Next, open Benchmark to see the results. Clicking Calibration complete lets you rerun the calibration. Rerunning deletes the current benchmark and energy audit results, and you’ll need to check inputs and run the calibration again.

29.title: What the calibration matches
29.content: The calibration runs the model hundreds of times, changing its inputs (schedules, setpoints, internal loads, envelope and HVAC settings) to find the combination that best matches your meter data. Every input is searched, including the schedules and setpoints you entered; the search starts from your values. | Hourly data - Every hour of electricity, scored as CV(RMSE) + 3 × |NMBE|. Bias counts three times because its Guideline 14 limit is a third of CV(RMSE)’s (10% against 30%). The model also has to match the weather-driven part of your electricity, which InverseAudit separates from the schedule-driven part in your data, so the two are split the way your building splits them. Chilled water and steam meter data count when you upload them. | Monthly data - Each month’s kWh against Guideline 14 (CV(RMSE) and NMBE), the seasonal shape of the year, and peak demand. | Gas and fuel bills - The year’s total, or each month when the bills are actual meter readings. They count for at most a quarter of the score. | . The model runs with your meter year’s actual weather: hourly temperatures, humidity, wind, solar radiation, cloud cover and station pressure. Any hours without measured weather are filled from a typical year: TMYx 2011-2025 from the nearest weather station (CWEC in Canada). Buildings that already have a TMY3 typical year keep it. The benchmark and savings use the typical year. Times are in the building’s local standard time throughout. See Supported data formats.

30.title: If something goes wrong
30.content: The Check inputs button is grayed out One of the four cards is still incomplete, or you aren’t the building’s analyzer. The line under the button says which inputs are missing. I need to stop the calibration Click the progress button and confirm with Stop Calibration. The progress is lost, but your inputs are kept, so you can run it again. If it just started, wait about 10 seconds before stopping it. CV(RMSE) or NMBE is outside the limits Check the meter data for gaps or outliers and confirm the systems and schedules. See Read the calibration results. Check inputs warns that a utility rate is far from what the bills cost A rate you entered is more than 25% off the average cost per unit on your bills. Savings are priced at that rate. If the bills’ costs are complete, open the Rates card and click Use the bills’ rate. See Rates from your bills. The warning doesn’t stop the calibration. Check inputs warns that a gas bill looks skipped With Bills are actual meter readings ticked, a month billed 0 between months with gas is usually a reading the utility skipped and added to the next bill, and the month-by-month comparison would chase it. Correct the bills, or untick the option so the calibration fits the year’s total. See Natural gas and fuel oil. "Calibration failed" Your inputs are saved. Run the calibration again. If it fails a second time, contact support with the building’s name.

32.title: Cancel a subscription
32.content: Subscriptions renew automatically until you cancel them. For: Subscriber (the building's owner)Where: Home › Building setup › Subscription .

34.title: What you’ll see next
34.content: When you cancel at any point during your monthly or annual cycle, the building stays active until the end of the current billing period and won’t renew after that. Past payments are not refunded. Only the subscriber (the building’s owner) can cancel the subscription. After an ownership transfer, that’s the new owner. Other people see the button grayed out.

44.title: Costs, payback and incentives
44.content: How InverseAudit prices each measure, which utility incentives it applies, and how payback and SIR are calculated. For: AnalyzerWhere: Dataset › Retrofit Costs, Dataset › Utility Incentives and the Energy Auditing page . On this page . | Retrofit costs . | Create your own costs table | Change the cost of one measure | . | Utility incentives | Payback and SIR | Related | .

45.title: Retrofit costs
45.content: The cost of each measure comes from a retrofit costs table, priced per unit (for example per square foot of roof). Open Dataset › Retrofit Costs in the left menu to see it. When you click Update, the audit prices the measures with your own table for the building’s audit year and state if you have one, and otherwise the Standard dataset. The standard dataset can’t be edited. Calculate only recalculates the savings; the costs, the number of measures and the net project budget are recalculated when you click Update. | Column | Meaning | . | Life Expectancy | Years the measure lasts. Used for the SIR. | . | Bare Material | Material cost per unit, without overhead and profit | . | Bare Labor | Labor cost per unit, without overhead and profit | . | Bare Total Costs | Bare material + bare labor | . | Multiplier | Overhead and profit markup. A blank multiplier counts as 1. | . | Total O&P | Bare Total Costs × Multiplier, the cost per unit used in the audit | . Create your own costs table . | On Retrofit Costs, click NEW COSTS TABLE. | Choose the audit year and state the table is for. | Choose Copy from a standard dataset, Copy from your dataset or Create an empty dataset, and click Create Table. | Edit the costs, then click Save changes. The bare total and Total O&P columns update when the page reloads. | . Each year and state can have one table. Make the table for the building’s own state, because the audit only picks up a table whose state matches the building. Change the cost of one measure . On the Recommendations tab of the report, the analyzer can click a measure’s Retrofit Costs or Utility Incentives value, enter a new amount and click Update. A retrofit cost you type in is kept the next time you update the report. All other costs are priced again from the current retrofit costs table.

46.title: Utility incentives
46.content: Open Dataset › Utility Incentives and choose the Utility, Service Rate and Audit Year to see the incentive programs InverseAudit knows about. This page is maintained by InverseAudit. If your utility’s programs are missing or out of date, click Contact Us. | Performance-based incentives pay per kWh and per kW saved. These are the ones the audit calculates. | Retrofit-based incentives are listed with their program name and website for reference. They aren’t added to the audit’s totals. | The Whole building tab holds programs that pay for the whole building’s savings or per square foot. | . Incentives need a utility rate. With an average rate, the Net project budget card says that incentives can’t be applied. See Rates. In the Energy Audit, the Net project budget card shows the retrofit cost after incentives. Under its Manage menu, the analyzer chooses the Incentive Method: Measure-based or Whole building. Only methods the utility offers can be chosen. Portfolio and the report use the same method. Whole-building incentives add the Performance row (per kWh and kW saved) and the Building Area row (per ft²) when their switches are on. When the program sets a Max Limit (%), the building-area part is limited to that share of the project budget.

47.title: Payback and SIR
47.content: | Value | Formula | Where | . | Payback period | Cost of measures ÷ annual cost savings | Payback period card, Summary tab | . | Net payback period | (Cost of measures − incentives) ÷ annual cost savings | Summary tab, when there are incentives | . | SIR | Annual cost savings × life expectancy ÷ (retrofit cost − incentive) | Recommendations tab | . Savings aren’t discounted. An SIR above 1 means the measure pays for itself over its life. A payback under 30 years shows a green flag on the card. 59.title: Electricity
59.content: kW and kWh in interval meter data . Interval meter data typically presents energy consumption information in two key metrics: kilowatts (kW) and kilowatt-hours (kWh). Proper interpretation of these metrics is crucial for accurate energy analysis and billing. Definitions . | kW (kilowatt): A measure of power, representing the rate of energy consumption at a given moment. | kWh (kilowatt-hour): A measure of energy, representing the total amount of electricity consumed over a period of time. | . Data conversion . When converting interval data to hourly figures: . | kW values are averaged to represent the mean power demand. | kWh values are summed to represent the total energy consumption. | . Critical Interpretation . Misinterpreting kW as kWh or vice versa can lead to significant errors in energy calculations: . | If 30-minute kW intervals are treated as kWh, annual energy consumption is overestimated by 100% (double the actual kWh). | If 30-minute kWh intervals are treated as kW, annual energy consumption is underestimated by 50% (half the actual kWh). | . These errors, when propagated over extended periods, can result in substantial discrepancies in energy analysis. Data formats for InverseAudit . InverseAudit supports two major data formats: Green Button and CSV. This manual outlines the specifications for each format and how they are handled by the system. Green Button format . The Green Button is a standardized data format designed for easy and secure access to energy usage data. | Format: Standardized, machine-readable | Purpose: Allows utility customers to access their energy usage data in a consumer-friendly format | Handling: InverseAudit reads each reading’s unit and multiplier from the file (Wh or kWh, energy or power), adds 15-minute readings up into hours, and uses electricity readings only. If the building exports solar power, the hourly use is the energy delivered minus the energy sent back to the grid. Times are converted from UTC to the building’s local standard time. | One file per year: a year split across several XML files, or a zipped download, isn’t read. Unzip it, and use one file that covers the year. | . CSV (comma-separated values) format . CSV is a common output format for spreadsheet programs. InverseAudit supports two types of CSV formats and can automatically recognize the type. Horizontal CSV format . | Structure: Horizontal header shows time, First column shows date | Default Unit: kW | Unit Specification: If needed, include “kWh” or “kW” in the first cell of the first column | File Extension: .csv | . Vertical CSV format . InverseAudit supports two variations of the vertical format: . Two-column format . | Column 1: Date and time combined | Column 2: Electricity usage data | . Three-column format . | Column 1: Date | Column 2: Time | Column 3: Electricity usage data | . Data import process . InverseAudit automatically detects the format of the imported file (Green Button or CSV). For CSV files, the system determines whether it’s a horizontal or vertical format. The data is then processed according to the identified format. Best practices . | Keep the data consistent within each file. | For CSV files, keep the structure described above. | With the horizontal CSV format, specify the unit (kW or kWh) if it differs from the default. | . Times and daylight saving . InverseAudit works in the building’s local standard time throughout: the meter data, the weather and the model. Each reading belongs to the hour it ends in. | CSV files can be in standard time or in clock time (with daylight saving). A file with no readings in the hour that’s skipped in spring counts as clock time and is moved to standard time automatically. | Green Button files are in UTC and are converted. | The model applies daylight saving to the building’s schedules where the location observes it, so the HVAC still starts at the clock time people come in. | The charts on Home show standard time, so in summer a reading appears an hour earlier than on a wall clock. | .

77.doc: Scenarios and the energy use gap
77.title: Compared scenarios
77.content: All benchmark results compare three versions of your building, all derived from the calibrated model: . |   | Scenario | What it is | . | A | Current building performance | Your building as it operates today | . | B | Typical operation scenario | The same building with typical schedules and setpoints | . | C | Code-compliant scenario | The same building built to the selected energy code | . Both gaps are measured from your building against different scenarios, so they overlap and don’t add up. A negative gap means your building does better than that scenario.

91.title: Terms
91.content: . | Analyzer: The person who enters the building’s data, runs the calibration and performs the energy audit. Other people the building is shared with see it in view-only mode. See Roles and the analyzer. | ASHRAE Guideline 14: A guideline for measuring energy savings. Its CV(RMSE) and NMBE limits are used to judge whether a calibrated model fits the meter data. | ASHRAE Level 1 audit: A brief audit, as ASHRAE Standard 211 defines it: the building and its energy use, a benchmark and target, and low-cost and capital measures with qualitative estimates. It includes a site visit by a qualified energy auditor. See The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports. | ASHRAE Level 2 audit: An energy survey and engineering analysis, as ASHRAE Standard 211 defines it, that identifies energy conservation measures with their savings and cost estimates. It includes a site visit by a qualified energy auditor. See The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports. | ASHRAE Standard 211: The standard for commercial building energy audits (ANSI/ASHRAE/ACCA Standard 211). It defines Level 1, Level 2 and Level 3 audits and what their reports contain. | Asset gap: The energy a building uses above the code-compliant scenario because of its design, envelope and equipment (B - C). | Asset score: A rating of a building’s as-built physical characteristics and energy systems, independent of occupancy and operation. It compares the calibrated model with the same building built to the selected energy code: 100 - 50 × A / C. | Audit report: The report produced on the Energy Auditing page, with the Summary, Analysis, Recommendations and Utility analysis tabs. It can be downloaded as PDF. | Average rate: A single rate per unit of energy, used when your utility’s rate structure isn’t selected. With an average rate, demand cost savings and utility incentives aren’t calculated. Also called a blended rate. | Baseline: The building’s calibrated energy model: its meter data, geometry, systems and rates, run through the calibration. A building has a baseline once it’s calibrated. | Calibration: The process that tunes the building’s energy model until it matches the meter data. See Check inputs and run calibration. | Calibration length: How long the calibration searches for the best fit: Quick (about 3 minutes), Standard (about 20 minutes, recommended) or Thorough (about 40 minutes). | Client: A company you share audits with. Its contacts sign in with I’m reviewing an audit report and see the posted audits of buildings assigned to the company. | Climate zone: A geographic region defined by ASHRAE standards, characterized by similar weather patterns, used to determine the energy code requirements. | Compared scenarios (A, B, C): The three versions of the building used on the Benchmark page, all derived from the calibrated model. A is the building as it operates today, B is the same building with typical schedules and setpoints, and C is the same building built to the selected energy code. | CV(RMSE): A statistical measure of how much the model’s results vary from the measured data: the root mean squared error divided by the mean of the measured data. A lower value means a better fit. ASHRAE Guideline 14 accepts up to 30% for hourly data and 15% for monthly data. | End-use analysis: A breakdown of energy use by category within a building, such as lighting, heating, cooling or plug loads. | Energy conservation measure (ECM): A specific action or upgrade that reduces a building’s energy use or improves its efficiency. | Energy use gap: How much more energy the building uses than the code-compliant scenario (A - C), split into the asset gap and the operational gap. See Scenarios and the energy use gap. | Energy use intensity (EUI): A building’s annual energy use divided by its floor area, usually in kBtu/ft². | ENERGY STAR score: A 1-100 rating of a building’s energy efficiency compared with similar buildings nationwide. Higher is better, and 50 is the median. | Green Button: A standardized XML format for downloading energy use data from a utility. | Interval data: Meter data recorded every 15, 30 or 60 minutes, usually by a smart meter or a BEMS. | Lighting power density: Installed lighting power per floor area, in W/ft². | Net payback period: The cost of the measures minus incentives, divided by the annual cost savings. | NMBE: A statistical measure of the model’s overall bias: the mean difference between measured and simulated data, divided by the mean of the measured data. A value closer to zero is better. ASHRAE Guideline 14 accepts within ±10% for hourly data and ±5% for monthly data. | Operational gap: The energy a building uses above the typical operation scenario because of its schedules, setpoints and operating practice (A - B). | Operational score: A rating of how the building is operated. It compares the calibrated model with the same building run on typical (ASHRAE) schedules: 100 - 50 × A / B. | Payback period: The time it takes for a measure’s savings to equal its cost. | Performance-based incentive: A utility incentive paid per kWh and per kW saved. | Post / Unpost: Posting shares the audit report with the building’s client and adds the building to Portfolio. Unposting hides the report again so you can make changes. | R-value: A material’s thermal resistance, in ft²·h·°F/Btu. Higher is better insulated. | Savings-to-investment ratio (SIR): A measure’s savings over its lifetime divided by its net cost (retrofit cost minus incentives). InverseAudit doesn’t discount future savings. | Setback temperature: A less strict temperature setting used during unoccupied periods to save energy while keeping minimal comfort. | Setpoint temperature: The temperature the HVAC system maintains during occupied periods. | Site EUI: The energy used on site per floor area, in kBtu/ft² per year. | Source EUI: Site energy plus the losses from producing and delivering it, per floor area. ENERGY STAR uses source energy. | Subscriber: The building’s owner: the person who created it, or the new owner after a transfer. The subscriber subscribes and cancels, and assigns the analyzer. | U-value: The rate of heat transfer through a building element, in Btu/h·ft²·°F. Lower is better insulated. | Weather normalization: Adjusting energy use for weather, so different periods or locations can be compared fairly. | Whole-building energy model: A simulation of the building’s energy performance as one system, including climate, envelope and mechanical systems. | .

94.content: . | What it is: The calibrated model run with a typical year’s weather: TMYx 2011-2025 from the nearest weather station (CWEC in Canada), or TMY3 for buildings that already use it. | How it’s used: For consistent energy analysis across different time periods. | .

95.title: Two reference models
95.content: The scores compare your building with two versions of itself: . | Typical Operation Scenario (B) - Your building with standard operating schedules and setpoints. It shows how much of your energy use comes from how the building is operated. The schedules for lighting, equipment, occupancy, HVAC and hot water come from the ASHRAE Standard 90.1-2007 User’s Manual (Appendix G) for the building type. The setpoints are 76 °F cooling and 72 °F heating while the HVAC runs, and 90 °F and 55 °F while it’s off. | Code-Compliant Scenario (C) - Your building built to just meet the selected energy code. It shows how much comes from the building itself: its envelope and equipment. | . On the Benchmark page, your building as it operates today is the Current Building Performance (A). Both scores use a scale where 100 means using no energy and 50 means using exactly as much as the reference scenario. Higher is better. Operational score . | Reference: Typical Operation Scenario (B), using standard (ASHRAE) schedules instead of the actual operating conditions | Formula: Operational score = 100 - 50 × A EUI / B EUI | . Asset score . | Reference: Code-Compliant Scenario (C), with the input parameters changed to meet the selected energy code | Formula: Asset score = 100 - 50 × A EUI / C EUI | .

104.content: The Benchmarking page shows how your calibrated building performs today and where its energy goes. 127.title: Meter data
127.content: The calibration matches the model to your meter data, so its quality decides how accurate the results are. For: AnalyzerWhere: Home › Meter Data card . 128.title: Steps
128.content: . | On Home, click the building’s Meter data card. | Add the electricity data: . | Hourly data - On the first tab, Import files, drop your interval data file into the upload area and click Import and fill meter data. See Natural gas and fuel oil. If the building uses district chilled water or steam, upload its 60-minute data on the Chilled water or Steam tab. | Click Save changes. | . 130.title: Import utility bills with AI
130.content: The first tab can fill in the fields for you. Upload your utility bills (and, for buildings with hourly data, your interval data file) and click Import and fill monthly data (buildings with monthly data, tab Import bills) or Import and fill meter data (buildings with hourly data, tab Import files). Check the values on the other tabs before you save. The import reads each bill’s usage, peak demand and total cost. The costs set your utility rates: see Rates from your bills. You can upload up to 50 files of up to 40 MB each: PDF, JPG, PNG, XLS, XLSX, CSV, TXT or XML (Green Button), with at most two CSV or TXT files and one Excel file. Importing again overwrites the data on the other tabs.

131.title: Natural gas and fuel oil
131.content: Enter each month’s use on the Natural gas / fuel oil tab: therms for natural gas, gallons for fuel oil. Purchased steam without a meter file is entered here too, in MMBtu. The two options beside the table decide how the calibration uses these bills: . | No natural gas or fuel oil - Sets every month to 0. Tick it only when the building uses neither. If the building heats with gas and you leave its bills out, its heating isn’t calibrated. | Bills are actual meter readings - Tick it when every bill is an actual reading, with no estimated, skipped or combined months. The calibration then compares each month’s bill with the model, against ASHRAE Guideline 14. Left unticked, it fits the year’s total. This option isn’t offered for fuel oil, whose deliveries don’t follow the months. | . Utilities sometimes skip a month’s reading and bill it with the next one. Enter 0 for the skipped month, not an estimate, and leave Bills are actual meter readings unticked: the year’s total is still right, so the calibration isn’t misled. With the option ticked, Check Inputs warns about a month billed 0 between two months with gas. The calibration weighs electricity more than gas: gas counts for at most a quarter of the score. Gas bills are usually further from anything a model can match than electricity. The audit report’s Appendix A states whether the gas was calibrated to each month or to the year’s total.

132.title: Missing data and outliers
132.content: Treat readings that don’t represent actual energy use as missing data. Up to 2,500 hours of data points can be missing, and the data must cover at least 9 months. To exclude readings, edit the file in Excel or any text editor and either: . | remove the entire row, including the date, or | fill the readings with zeros or blanks, keeping the dates. | . The examples below are all acceptable in a CSV (comma-separated values) file. For Green Button data, use an XML editor. .

133.title: If something goes wrong
133.content: My interval data file won't import Check that the file matches one of the supported data formats, and that it covers at least 9 months with no more than 2,500 missing hours. If it still won’t import, contact support and attach the file. The annual electricity use looks doubled or halved The file’s unit was probably read as kW instead of kWh, or the other way around. 157.title: ENERGY STAR score
157.content: The ENERGY STAR score rates your building’s overall energy performance on a 1 to 100 scale, reflecting its physical assets, how it’s operated and how it’s used. A score of 50 is the median: lower is worse than similar buildings nationwide, and higher is better. It helps you decide which buildings to improve first.1 . The card shows your building’s score and site EUI next to the portfolio median (a score of 50) and its site EUI. The site EUI uses the modeled floor area, so it matches the calibrated model. If the model changes, for example after you rerun the calibration, the score is recalculated the next time you open the page. To calculate the score for a different property type, choose it under ENERGY STAR property type and click the refresh button next to it. Some building types aren’t covered by ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager, and no score is shown for them.

158.title: Operational and asset scores
158.content: The operational score and the asset score work like the ENERGY STAR score: 50 means the same energy use as the reference, a lower score is worse, and a higher score is better. Both compare your building with a version of itself rather than with other buildings. | Operational score - Compares the calibrated model with the same building run on typical schedules based on ASHRAE standards. For example, if an office building runs longer than the typical Monday to Friday, 8 am to 5 pm schedule, its operational score is lower than 50. Operational score = 100 - 50 × A / B | Asset score - Similar to the miles-per-gallon (MPG) rating used for cars. It compares the calibrated model with the same building built to the selected energy code (ASHRAE Standard 90.1): roof and exterior wall insulation, window U-values and SHGC, and heating and cooling efficiencies. Asset score = 100 - 50 × A / C | . A, B and C are the three compared scenarios. Scores range from 0 to 100. The scores are calculated with weather-normalized models, which use typical weather (TMY3) in place of the actual weather data. See How scores are calculated.

159.title: Energy cost vs. energy code
159.content: Current performance vs. energy code shows how much higher or lower your building’s energy cost is than the code-compliant scenario, and how the current energy cost is split between energy sources. To compare with a different code, click the energy code’s name and choose another one. The results are recalculated, which can take up to 10 seconds. The code currently in force in your state is tagged Current State Code. Only the building’s analyzer can change the code.

182.title: What InverseAudit does
182.content: InverseAudit is an energy auditing platform for commercial buildings. It builds a calibrated energy model of your building from monthly or interval meter data, without the effort that manual modeling and calibration require.

183.title: The workflow
183.content: graph LR A["Add a building"] --> B["Enter data"] B --> C["Calibrate"] C --> D["Benchmark"] D --> E["Subscribe"] E --> F["Energy audit"] F --> G["Post the report"] . | Add your building. | Enter its meter data, geometry, systems and rates. | Run the calibration. InverseAudit tunes the model until it matches your meter data. | Review the benchmark results. | Subscribe the building to unlock the energy audit. | In the energy audit, try energy conservation measures and see their savings and payback. | Post the report so your contacts and clients can see it. | .

184.title: Why a model should be calibrated
184.content: Energy modeling is not always accurate, especially for older existing buildings. A model’s accuracy is limited by the complexity of buildings. It also depends on operational factors such as schedules and occupancy, how systems and equipment are operated, plug loads and weather.1 A model that hasn’t been calibrated with utility data isn’t accurate, so it should be calibrated before energy cost savings are calculated.

185.title: Why use InverseAudit
185.content: . | It creates and calibrates a model based on your utility data and historical weather data. This leads to an accurate and representative model of your building. | Its analysis has the depth of an ASHRAE Level 2 energy audit: savings and costs for each measure, calculated with a calibrated model. | With the ASHRAE Level 1 or Level 2 report and a site visit by a qualified energy auditor, the report can meet ASHRAE Standard 211 for that level. | . InverseAudit can be used for: . | ASHRAE Standard 211 Level 2 energy audits, with a site visit by a qualified energy auditor | Energy audits for building-ordinance requirements (the audit report; filing happens outside InverseAudit) | LEED O+M: Existing Buildings | .

186.title: Methodologies and standards
186.content: InverseAudit incorporates industry standards such as: . | ASHRAE Standard 90.1 | ASHRAE Standard 211 | IPMVP (International Performance Measurement and Verification Protocol) | . It combines them with its own calibration methods. See How scores are calculated for the models behind the results. To try it, follow the Quick start with the Demo Building. | How Accurate is Energy Modeling in the Market. ↩ . | .
